sections.title: Does Phantom Blade Zero Have a Map?
sections.content:
Yes, but not the kind the question usually means. Phantom Blade Zero has no world map screen: there is no single image of the Wulin you can zoom out to. What it has is one hand-painted ink-wash map per region, a minimap that fills in as you explore, and a bell network that acts as the fast-travel layer.

So the three questions behind "phantom blade zero map" have three separate answers:

  • Is there a map? Yes - per region, with fog of war and a completion percentage.
  • Is it open world? No. S-GAME's own wording is that every corner is handcrafted and the game is neither open-world nor a straight line. Community documentation calls the structure wide-linear with light Metroidvania-style exploration.
  • How many maps? Nine region blocks in the boss data. Public counts vary between eight, nine and ten because sites disagree on whether Mirage Estate and the endgame count as their own regions. The table below uses the boss data's grouping so the counts reconcile with the boss list and the boss order.

If what you actually want is the region-to-region progression order, the locations page covers that in narrative form. This page is about the map system itself: how big it is, how the bells work, what each map hides, and what locks when.

sections.title: How Big Is the Map?
sections.content:
There is no square-kilometre figure, and any number quoted for one is an estimate. What can be counted is what sits on the maps: 60 named encounters across nine region blocks - 34 on the story path and 26 optional, recurring or rematch fights - plus 34 weapons and Phantom Edges with a recorded pickup location.

The shape matters more than the size. Regions are joined seamlessly rather than through a level select, so the boundary between two maps is a corridor, not a menu. Backtracking is done through bells, which means the map is effectively a network of hubs rather than one continuous surface - and that is why per-map completion percentages exist at all.

Two structural details decide how much of each map you will actually see. First, some areas need a particular Phantom Edge to reach, so a map can read 80% complete while a quarter of it is still physically closed to you. Second, bells clear fog around the bell rather than around you, so a map you have crossed twice can still have dark corners that no amount of walking fixes.

sections.content:
Counts are encounters, not characters - Pangzhen has eleven because it is the hub players return to, not because eleven strangers stand in the street. sections.title: The Bells Are the Map
sections.content:
Bells do four jobs, and only one of them is fast travel. Treating them as waypoints undersells the system and is why people finish a region at 70% and cannot work out what they missed.

  1. Fog reveal. The first touch clears the minimap around that bell. Walking past a dark area does not reveal it - the bell does.
  2. Fast travel. Travel runs between bells you have already touched. There is no free travel across the whole map, which is what keeps the wide-linear structure from behaving like an open world.
  3. Restock. Combat resources refresh at bells, the same way a bonfire or a lantern does in the games this one is inevitably compared to.
  4. Gating. Some fights are built into the travel network itself - forced-combat waypoints you cannot walk around. A bell that will not let you leave until a fight ends is not a bug.

Water travel exists as a second traversal method in at least one region; the boat crossing on Meigu Lake is part of the map, not a cutscene. The collectibles page covers what the bells are worth in completion terms.

sections.title: Map Completion: What the Percentage Counts
sections.content:
Each map tracks three things: the total number of collectibles in it, the specific pickups you have and have not taken, and a completion percentage. The categories that count are special items (Sha-chi Amber shards, Black Stone shards, Memory Flowers), books and story items. Weapons, flasks, accessories and Remnant Spark are equipment or currency and do not move the number.

That split is why a map can sit at 95% with nothing visibly left. The usual culprits, in order of how often they are the answer:

  • A bell you touched but never searched around - the fog is gone, the pickup is not.
  • An area behind a Phantom Edge you have not found yet, so the map still marks it as locked.
  • An optional fight whose arena held a story item, and the fight expired at the climb.

The three permanent upgrades are worth chasing for their own sake: Sha-chi Amber raises the Sha-chi bar cap, Black Stone raises attack and poise-break, Memory Flowers raise maximum health. Exact totals per map are not published anywhere, including here - the in-game counter is the only authority.

sections.title: What Locks at Mount Soulrend
sections.content:
Mount Soulrend is the point of no return, and it locks optional content rather than story. Anything still open behind you - optional fights, their drops, side tales - expires on the climb. For the story itself nothing is lost; for a 100% run the last region is where you either did the work or did not.

Practical order for a completion run: finish Pangzhen's optional fights before leaving it (it carries the most), do Meigu Lake's optional block because one fight there gates the true ending, and check the missables page before starting the ascent. The trophy guide lists which trophies sit behind that gate.

sections.title: Interactive Maps vs This Page
sections.content:
If you want to pixel-hunt a single chest, an interactive map with pins is the right tool - MapGenie, the Fextralife map and the Game8 map all do that, and this site does not host one. What an interactive map does not do is tell you the order to do things in, which is what this page and boss order are for.
